titel: Ignatiana: An Introduction to a Research Apparatus for Ignatian Spirituality
note: Author note: This essay serves as a stand-alone introduction to the digital research apparatus *Ignatiana: A Research Apparatus for Ignatian Spirituality* and as introductory text for the site itself. paras: In the first of the twenty *Annotations* that open the *Spiritual Exercises*, Ignatius of Loyola explains his title by an analogy. Just as walking, travelling and running are bodily exercises, so every way of preparing the soul “to rid itself of all disordered affections” and then “to seek and find the divine will” in the ordering of a life is a spiritual exercise (SpEx [1]; Ignatius of Loyola, 1919). The definition is deliberately unglamorous. It describes not a doctrine but a practice, and a practice that has to be *given*—by one person to another, over roughly a month, with a great deal of apparatus about posture, timetable, diet and the interpretation of inner states. What Ignatius set in motion at Manresa in 1522, and kept revising until his death in 1556, was less a book than a method for producing decisions; the book is its manual (Ganss, 1992; O’Malley, 1993).

*Ignatiana: A Research Apparatus for Ignatian Spirituality* (Fassbender, 2026a) is a digital instrument built around that manual and the texts through which its method became the practice of an order. At its centre stand the founder’s own writings: the *Exercises*, in a trilingual public-domain parallel edition of the Spanish Autograph, the Latin *Vulgata* of 1548 and Elder Mullan’s English of 1914; the *Constitutions*; the dictated memoir known as *A Pilgrim’s Testament*; the *Spiritual Diary* of 1544–1545; and twenty-four letters of 1524–1547 in full. Around them stand the texts in which the *Exercises* were taught and administered—the Society’s *Official Directory* of 1599, bilingual, and the *Memoriale* of Pierre Favre, the first companion, whom Ignatius judged the finest giver of the *Exercises*—and, in further lines, the Society in the world before 1773, the conscience of Friedrich Spee, and the counter-voices, from the forged *Monita secreta* to the brief with which Clement XIV dissolved the order. Every paragraph carries its canonical number; a concordance searches the whole corpus at once; a lexicon follows the vocabulary of consolation, desolation and election as it migrates from the manual into the journal, the law and the letters; and a citation-bound dialogue answers questions only from passages it can cite.

The history of the Society of Jesus and the study of its founder have been written thoroughly and well—as institutional history (O’Malley, 1993, 2014), as a doctrine of the spiritual life (de Guibert, 1964), as commentary on the rules of discernment (Toner, 1982), as a psychology of a saint (Meissner, 1992), and as textual criticism of the memoir on which so much of the rest depends (McManamon, 2013). What has been harder to come by, for any reader who is not inside a Jesuit library, is the evidence in a form that can be cited to the paragraph and searched across works. The primary texts are dispersed across the hundred-odd volumes of the *Monumenta Historica Societatis Iesu*, across nineteenth-century printings of unequal reliability, and across modern translations which are excellent and in copyright. The premise of this apparatus is the premise of its sibling, *Calculemus* (Fassbender, 2026b): that a tradition deserves what classical philology has always given its sources—exact citation, a stated editorial method, and the standing possibility of checking a claim against the sentence that grounds it. This essay introduces the corpus: the five lines along which it is organized, the argument that runs through them, the reason the collection ends where it does, and the way the apparatus is to be used and not to be trusted.

abschnitte.titel: The Founder: Manual, Law, Memoir, Journal, Letters
paras: The first line of the corpus is the founder’s own hand and dictation, and it is best read as five genres rather than five books. The *Exercises* are a manual, addressed largely to the director rather than to the person making the retreat; most of their 370 numbered paragraphs are instruction, outline, timetable or rule. Their four Weeks—stages, not calendar weeks—move from the recognition of disorder through contemplation of the life, passion and resurrection of Christ toward an *election*, a decision about how one’s life is to be ordered (SpEx [23], [91], [136], [175]). The technical core of the method is the set of rules for the discernment of spirits (SpEx [313]–[336]), which define consolation and desolation and prescribe conduct under each; the vocabulary they fix is the vocabulary that every later text in the corpus assumes (Toner, 1982). The book was approved by Paul III in 1548 in the polished Latin of the *Vulgata*; the Spanish Autograph, a copy of about 1544 with corrections in Ignatius’s hand, remained the working text of the Society and is the base of the modern critical edition (Dalmases, 1969; Ganss, 1992).

The *Constitutions* are the institutional translation of the *Exercises*—law of an unusual kind, in which prescriptions alternate with *Declarations* that explain, soften or qualify them, and in which the whole body of legislation is prefaced by the admission that written rules matter less than “the interior law of charity and love” (Const [134]; Padberg, 1996). Drafted by Ignatius with his secretary Juan de Polanco between about 1547 and 1556 and approved by the first general congregation in 1558, they follow a member’s life from admission through formation, incorporation, mission and government to the preservation of the whole body. The chapter on obedience (Const [547]) is the most cited and most polemicized passage in the corpus; the *Declaration* on choosing missions by greater need, greater fruit and the more universal good (Const [622]) is the closest the corpus comes to an explicit method of apostolic priority. In the present edition two texts share every page: the sixteenth-century *Constitutions* in bracketed numbers and the modern *Complementary Norms* in plain ones, and the apparatus treats only the former as a citation series.

The memoir is the strangest of the five. It is not an autobiography but a narrative extracted under pressure: between 1553 and 1555 Ignatius yielded to Jerónimo Nadal’s urging and told his story in irregular sittings to Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, who listened, made notes afterwards from memory, and later dictated a fuller text partly in Spanish and partly in Italian (Divarkar, 1995; Munitiz & Endean, 1996). Ignatius speaks of himself throughout in the third person as “the pilgrim.” The account runs only from the wound at Pamplona in 1521 to the founding years in Rome, and it is shaped: McManamon (2013) has shown that it follows the conventions of a conversion narrative modelled on Luke–Acts, selecting episodes to teach discernment rather than to document a life. Its value lies in being the only sustained first-person account of the experiences that produced the *Exercises*—the convalescent noticing that daydreams of the world leave him dry while thoughts of imitating the saints leave him content (Autobiog. [8]), the crisis of scruples at Manresa (Autobiog. [23]), the illumination beside the Cardoner of which he can report no content, only that everything seemed new (Autobiog. [30])—and in da Câmara’s direct question, at the end, about how the book was composed (Autobiog. [99]).

The *Spiritual Diary* is the one text Ignatius wrote for no reader but himself, and it reads accordingly: abbreviations, private sigla, tallies of tears, sentences that break off. Two small autograph gatherings survive from February 1544 to February 1545, almost certainly a fragment of something larger. The first tracks, day by day over forty days, a formal election about whether the Society’s professed houses might hold fixed income, with written arguments for and against poverty and daily notes on what he felt while offering each option; the second follows a year of daily Mass and the recurring phenomenon he calls *loquela* (Diary [1], [34], [222]; Munitiz, 1987). Scholars use it as the closest available approach to Ignatian discernment in operation rather than in prescription, and as a check on the more schematic account of the *Exercises*—which is why the apparatus places it beside the manual rather than after it.

The letters are the founder as correspondent and administrator. Ignatius wrote, or had Polanco write under his direction, nearly seven thousand surviving letters—the largest correspondence of any sixteenth-century figure (O’Malley, 1993). The apparatus carries in full the twenty-four selected and translated by D. F. O’Leary in 1914 (Ignatius of Loyola, 1914), chosen by their editors for what they reveal of the writer’s interior life rather than for administrative weight: counsel to a Catalan nun on false humility and excessive fear (Letters, no. 5); an endorsement of organized poor relief in his home town (no. 10); operating instructions for the first papal mission (no. 12) and for the theologians at Trent (no. 20); and the long letter to the students at Coimbra on fervour and its excesses (no. 24). Read against the *Rules for Discernment*, the counsel letters apply them informally; read against the *Constitutions*, the instructions improvise what the law later codified.

abschnitte.titel: The School of Discernment: The Manual’s Manual and a Journal in Practice
paras: The second line of the corpus asks a question the first cannot answer by itself: how a private method became a transmissible one. The *Exercises* say what is to be done; they say remarkably little about how a director is to administer it, and Ignatius left notes and dictations but no finished directory. After four decades of drafts by Polanco, Miró and others, a first official draft circulated in 1591 for comment and the definitive text was printed at Florence in 1599 with Claudio Acquaviva’s letter of promulgation (Palmer, 1996). The *Official Directory* is the manual’s manual. Its forty chapters walk the director through the whole arc—who is to be admitted and in what form, how meditations are proposed and accounts of them taken, how each Week is paced, how the election is prepared, safeguarded and concluded—and they fix the *Exercises* as an administered practice at the moment the tradition consolidated (Dir. 1599, Prooem. [4–6]). Its working rules are memorable because they are concrete: the director should point out the vein of ore with a finger and let the exercitant dig it out himself (c. VIII [1]); when things go well he should withdraw and let the Creator deal directly with the creature (c. VII [3]); whoever cannot reach indifference about riches and poverty is not to enter the election at all (c. XXIII [3]); and even a consoling motion must pass examination by reason illuminated by faith, because the angel of Satan transfigures himself into an angel of light (c. XXVIII [5]). The apparatus ships the Latin of the *Monumenta Ignatiana* (1919) with two English texts beside it: W. H. Longridge’s translation of the same year, and an unofficial working translation made for the site directly from the Latin. In either case, the rule is to cite the Latin.

Beside the manual’s manual stands a journal in which the rules are not expounded but used. Pierre Favre—the Savoyard shepherd boy who shared a room in Paris with Ignatius and Francis Xavier, the first priest of the Society, and the man Ignatius judged the finest giver of the *Exercises*—began his *Memoriale* at Speyer in June 1542 as a deliberate discipline: to note, day by day, the movements of devotion, desolation and desire that passed through him, so that nothing given should be lost (Favre, 1873, 1996). Several hundred dated entries follow, kept on the road through Germany, the Low Countries, Portugal and Spain until 1546, and they show what discernment looks like when nothing dramatic is happening: a desire examined, found subtly self-seeking, and reordered (Mem. [241]). Around the journal the volume preserves a retrospect of his life, an appendix of letters and counsels, and the celebrated instruction to Laínez on dealing with the heretics of the age—win the heart before arguing with the head (Mem. App. [382–388])—as well as the prayer list on which Luther, Melanchthon, Bucer and the Turk stand beside the pope and the emperor (Mem. [25]). Favre’s autograph is lost. What circulated in the Society was a transmitted Latin version, first made public by Marcel Bouix in 1873, the year after Favre’s beatification (Favre, 1873); the critical edition with the numbering scholarship now cites appeared only in the *Fabri Monumenta* of 1914. The apparatus rests, transparently, on the 1873 print, with a working translation and a paragraph numbering of its own—and it says so on every page.

The line now reaches beyond the founder: the apparatus carries Nadal’s annotations on the General Examen, in which the first authorized interpreter of the *Exercises* to the Society itself reads its vocation straight out of the meditations of the Kingdom and the Two Standards and gives the phrase that has defined Jesuit spirituality ever since — Ignatius ‘simul in actione contemplativus’, contemplative in action, finding God in all things (Nadal, 1919). Beside Nadal now stands Alonso Rodríguez: the Eighth Treatise of his *Practice of Perfection* of 1609, *Of Conformity to the Will of God*, carried complete in all thirty-four chapters — the school of discernment as a daily curriculum, read aloud in Jesuit novitiates for three centuries, and the direct ancestor of the Abandonment attributed to Caussade (Rodríguez, 1609, 1861). The English is the old translation printed at Dublin in 1861, made — as its title page states — not from the Spanish but from the French of the Abbé Régnier-Desmarais: the classic transmission chain of this book, carried as it stands. And the line now reaches its destination: the *Abandonment to Divine Providence* attributed to Jean-Pierre de Caussade — written before the suppression and printed long after it, in which the school is distilled to a single motion, the present moment as the sacrament of God’s will — is carried whole in Ramière’s arrangement of 1861, in Ella McMahon’s English of 1887 (Caussade, 1861, 1887): his doctrinal preface, the treatise in three books, and the appendix of pieces by Surin, Bossuet, Francis de Sales, de Chantal and La Colombière. The attribution is debated in modern scholarship, and the apparatus states it as debated: what is carried is, demonstrably, the text Ramière published under Caussade’s name. Behind the school's practice its doctrine now begins to be carried as well: the Ratio Studiorum of 1599, the pedagogical constitution of the order, stands in the apparatus in its rules for the professors of scholastic theology and of philosophy, complete and bilingual — the document that bound the schools to St. Thomas and to Aristotle in the same breath as it stated the Society's liberty, and the hinge to the De anima course itself — whose Coimbra commentary now follows: the Prooemium of the Conimbricenses' Commentarii in tres libros De anima, transcribed by eye from the 1617 printing and carried complete and bilingual, answers what the science of the soul is — the Delphic nosce te ipsum read as psychology, the soul as horizon aeternitatis et temporis, Augustine's two questions, and the disputed subject of Aristotle's three books, resolved in the college's characteristic both-ways manner (Conimbricenses, 1598/1617; Society of Jesus, 1599/1893). And above the course stands its greatest commentator: three chapters of Suárez's own De anima lectures, in the posthumous text completed by Baltasar Álvares, carry the strand to its point — the soul's powers really distinct from the soul yet flowing from it and rooted in it, the seven names of the inner sense reduced to a single power, and the intellect that in this life cannot work without a phantasm — the anthropology in which composing a place with the imagination is not a preliminary to the understanding's prayer but its condition (Suárez, 1621/1856).

With the second, cultural program the school gains its sound. Athanasius Kircher's *Musurgia universalis* (Rome, 1650)—written at the Collegio Romano and printed in the Jubilee year, a folio in two volumes that sat in the Society's colleges for a century—is carried in a deliberately narrow cut. The Synopsis of the ten books lays the whole architecture on a single page, from the physiology of natural sound to the *decachordon naturae*, whose tenth register is the music of the Archetype, God's concert with universal nature, the whole folded into one psalm verse. The voices of the birds from Book I make the nightingale 'as it were an Idea of all music'—and Kircher did both things his sentence promises: he transferred her clausulae into musical notes on Iconismus III, carried here as a page image with the cock, the laying hen, the quail and the cuckoo's minor third beneath her glottisms, and he dissected the bird, the plate and the scalpel in one chapter. And the doctrine of the affects from Book VII names the four conditions for moving the soul—harmony, number, the words' hidden energy, and the hearer's disposition, without which 'you will sooner move a rock than an indisposed man'—and closes with the program of renewing the miracles of ancient music by matching the mode to the temperament (Kircher, 1650). The module stands deliberately beside Muratori's chapter on the music of the Indians (Mur. IX): the same Society's music, theorized in Rome and practiced on the Paraná.

abschnitte.titel: The Society in the World: Mission, Observation, Self-Portrait
paras: The third line follows the *Exercises* out of the retreat house and across the world within a decade of their approval. The first shipped module is Francis Xavier: four letters carried complete in H. J. Coleridge’s translation of 1872, from Cochin, from Kagoshima, to Ignatius, and from Sancian, where Xavier died in 1552 within sight of China (Xavier, 1872). They are worth reading beside the *Constitutions*’ criteria for choosing missions, because they show the “more universal good” being weighed by a man on a beach, with a fever, and with no superior nearer than Rome. Beside Xavier now stands José de Acosta’s *Historia natural y moral de las Indias* — a Jesuit empiricism before the word, in which the New World is described by observation against the authorities — in eleven chapters of Edward Grimston’s English of 1604, carried in its own orthography (Acosta, 1590, 1880). Acosta crossed the equator, felt cold where Aristotle promised uninhabitable fire, and wrote down what could not be argued away: “what could I else do then, but laugh at Aristotle’s Meteors and his Philosophie?” The selection runs from that laughter through Potosí observed to the defence of the rationality of peoples who reckon without letters — the quipus read as registers, not as curiosities. And Ricci has followed: Trigault’s *De Christiana expeditione apud Sinas* is carried in the English reception of 1625 — Samuel Purchas’s digest “taken out of Ricius and Trigautius”, with the mission narrative and the death of Ricci (Ricci & Trigault, 1615, 1625/1906). The double transmission is itself part of the story: inculturation argued at the court of China — the change of habit from bonze to literatus, the *Booke of Friendship* written in Chinese, the burial place obtained of the emperor by petition — read through the eyes of a Protestant compiler, whose margins map his digest back to Trigault’s chapters. And with the *Relations* the line is complete: the order’s annual world-reporting of mission, ethnography and martyrdom, which became a genre, is carried in four selections of Thwaites’s edition and translation (Thwaites, 1896–1901) — Le Jeune wintering with the Montagnais, who opens the chapter with Epictetus as Acosta crossed the equator with Aristotle; Brébeuf’s *Instructions for the Fathers who shall be sent to the Hurons*, the accommodation rulebook of New France and the canoe-borne mirror of Ricci’s change of habit; and Ragueneau’s chapters of 1649 on the capture of Saint-Ignace and the deaths of Brébeuf and Lalemant, the register the genre was named for — each paragraph carrying Thwaites’s page number, the citation the scholarship uses.

The line closes with a self-portrait. In 1640 the Flemish-Belgian province published the *Imago primi saeculi Societatis Iesu* at the Plantin-Moretus press in Antwerp to mark the order’s first centenary: nearly a thousand folio pages of engraving, epigram and boast, the very book its critics would mock (Imago primi saeculi, 1640). The apparatus ships the engraved title and eleven of its emblems—one from each of the six books, with five deepenings—as page images, with the Latin distichs transcribed and working translations beside them—*Unus non sufficit orbis*, one world is not enough; *Da mihi animas*, give me souls—closes each emblem with its page from the *Af-Beeldinghe*, the Dutch counterpart issued by the same press in the same year, in which Adriaen Poirters glosses every lemma in a vernacular rhyme—and builds on them its iconographic reading path, which asks at every station what the rest of the corpus, looking over the emblem’s shoulder, would say. What does it mean that an order of “pilgrims” portrays itself as a throne? The emblem promises certainty; where do the election chapters admit difficulty? After the *Monita* and the *Provinciales*, does the emblem’s serenity read as confidence or as evasion? The centenary volume is carried as evidence of how the Society saw itself at one hundred, not as a verdict on whether it was right.

With the second, cultural program the world line gains the Society's boldest social experiment: the Reductions of Paraguay, carried in the two voices that brought them to Europe. Ludovico Antonio Muratori—no Jesuit, and he says so on his first page—compiled *Il cristianesimo felice* from the missionaries' letters; the module carries five chapters of the London English of 1759 complete, from the obstacles and the slaving raids of the Mamelucos (Mur. V) through the famous chapter on the music of the Indians (Mur. IX), the civil and the military government of the settlements (Mur. XV, XVIII), to the persecutions raised through envy (Mur. XX)—written a decade before the Treaty of Madrid turned those accusations into policy. Beside the outside admirer stands the protagonist: four bilingual passages of Antonio Ruiz de Montoya's *Conquista espiritual* (1639), the fleet of rafts and the three hundred canoes lost over the falls of the Paraná in the great exodus of 1631, and the deaths of Roque González and Alonso Rodríguez at Caaró, with the bell kept as a relic. The two witnesses correct each other: Muratori's happy Christianity read against Montoya's first person, thirty years in the missions and written for the court of Madrid.

The world line's second-program modules close their arc in Rome itself. Andrea Pozzo—lay brother, painter, and the Society's one canonised theorist of illusion—published the first volume of his *Perspectiva pictorum et architectorum* in 1693; the apparatus carries it in the London edition of 1707, which prints the Latin and an English translation on the same pages and opens with an Approbation signed by Christopher Wren, John Vanbrugh and Nicholas Hawksmoor—the English architectural establishment endorsing a Jesuit's book thirty years after the plot scares. The cut is the Sant'Ignazio dossier: the preface whose last sentence turns the punctum oculi into the Ignatian end itself—every line of the work drawn 'to that true Point, the Glory of GOD'; the Holy Week apparatus of the Forty Hours; the feigned dome painted on canvas in 1685, with the painter-friend who stood surety to repair at his own cost whatever fell if the painted corbels gave way; the plan of the church whose nave vault Pozzo was 'at present employ'd in painting'—the treatise catching the Apotheosis of St Ignatius in the act; and the Answer to the Objection, which defends the single determined point of sight and closes with the whole aesthetic in one clause: from its one point the art exhibits 'as upright, as flat, as concave, that which is not so' (Pozzo, 1707). With Pozzo the second program's three named modules stand complete, and the sixth reading path binds them: the Society as culture, from the Ratio's classrooms through Kircher's music and Pozzo's ceilings to the Reductions, the Imago and the court of China.

abschnitte.titel: The Conscience of the Society: Spee, and the Decree of 1593
paras: The fourth line began with a single author, and it stands on its own because it belongs to neither the school nor the critics: it is the order's conscience speaking from inside — first against a procedure the order's colleges served, and now also against a law the order gave itself. Friedrich Spee von Langenfeld, a Jesuit of the Rhineland, served as confessor to persons condemned for witchcraft and published in 1631, anonymously and against the wishes of his superiors, the *Cautio Criminalis*, a book on witch trials in which the procedure itself is put on trial: the torture that produces the confession that produces the next denunciation, and the impossibility, once accused, of proving innocence (Spee, 1631/2003). It is conscience from inside the order—the same trained attention to the motions of the soul that the *Exercises* teach, turned upon a legal machine and finding it demonic in the precise sense the rules of discernment give the word. The same conscience sings in the *Trutznachtigall*, the cycle of German religious poems published posthumously in 1649, of which the apparatus carries two complete — the lament of Christ on the Mount of Olives and the spring love-song of the soul for the absent Jesus (Spee, 1649). The apparatus now carries the *Cautio* itself: its opening question and its famous ending, Dubium LI, the numbered summa of the trials, complete in Latin with a working translation. The apparatus carries Spee as a line of his own because he is the corpus’s clearest evidence that the Ignatian formation could produce its own critic, and because a reader who has followed the discernment lexicon through the manual, the journal and the law should be able to test whether its vocabulary is in fact at work in a book about torture.

With the limpieza dossier the line gains its second front, and its hardest: not a voice against the world's institutions but the Society against itself. The early Society had refused the distinction of blood — Laínez, the second general, and Polanco, the founder's secretary, were of converso descent — and Ribadeneira's memorial preserves as eyewitness testimony what Ignatius said of it, before many and with tears in his eyes: that he would have counted it a special grace of God to be born of Jewish lineage — 'to be able to be a kinsman of Christ our Redeemer according to the flesh, and of the glorious Virgin Mary our Lady'. The Fifth General Congregation decreed the exclusion anyway in 1593, quoting the founder in support of what he had refused all his life, and recorded in its own decree book the three intercessions raised against it on the floor; Ribadeneira answered with thirteen numbered reasons, carried here complete — against the Constitutions, against the spirit of Ignatius, Laínez and Borja, against the honour of Spain, 'oil on the fire', Juan de Ávila's warning that distinction of lineages was one of the two things that could destroy the Society — down to the substance of the Institute itself (Ribadeneira, 1593/1923). The Sixth Congregation softened the bar to five generations in 1608 and, in the same decree, commanded silence on the matter; the impediment of origin stood until the 29th General Congregation removed it in 1946. The apparatus carries the decree, the dissent and the mitigation together, as it carries the Monita: as the debate, with the failure stated as failure (Maryks, 2010).

A corpus that collected only the Society’s own voices would be an apologia. The fifth line carries the case against, and it begins with a lie. The *Monita secreta*—the “secret instructions” by which the Society was alleged to acquire wealth, influence and widows’ estates—were composed in Kraków in 1614 by Hieronim Zahorowski, a dismissed Jesuit, and were reprinted in some form for three centuries in every language of Europe (Pavone, 2005). The apparatus carries them complete and bilingual from a hostile printing of 1857, with the Latin and English on facing pages as the alignment grid (Brownlee, 1857), and it carries them *as the debate, not as truth*—the forgery beside the texts it defames, so that a reader can see for themselves what the *Constitutions* actually say about property, obedience and the choice of missions, and what the pamphlet pretends they say. A forgery that forced a debate is evidence of the debate.

The second counter-voice is the most brilliant attack the Society ever received. Between January 1656 and March 1657 Blaise Pascal, writing anonymously for the Jansenist party of Port-Royal, published the eighteen *Lettres provinciales*, in which the casuistry of the Jesuit moral theologians—probabilism, the direction of intention, the doctrine of mental reservation—is exhibited in the words of its own authors and destroyed by ridicule (Pascal, 1656–1657/1856). The apparatus carries Letters V, VII and X complete in Thomas M’Crie’s translation of 1856, chosen because they are the letters in which the method of quotation is at its most exact and its most unfair. Pascal is the counter-voice that a student of Ignatian discernment most needs to read, because his charge is not that the Jesuits are wicked but that a method for finding God’s will in particulars will, in the hands of confessors eager to accommodate, become a method for finding permission.

The third counter-voice is not a voice but a verdict. On 21 July 1773 Clement XIV signed the brief *Dominus ac Redemptor*, dissolving the Society of Jesus in forty-one numbered paragraphs that rehearse, with studied moderation, two centuries of complaint and conclude that the order can no longer produce the abundant fruits for which it was founded (Clement XIV, 1773/1852). The apparatus carries the Latin complete in Theiner’s paragraph numbering with a working translation made for the site, because no full public-domain English translation of the brief could be located; it is the corpus’s intended closing text.

The corpus ends, deliberately, where a history of Ignatian spirituality would ordinarily turn a page. The Society of 1540–1773 is a completed object: the world in which the *Exercises* found their first practice, their official *Directory*, their missions and their enemies, bounded at one end by Paul III’s bull *Regimini militantis Ecclesiae* and at the other by Clement XIV’s brief. What lies beyond is named rather than carried: the brief of restoration, *Sollicitudo omnium ecclesiarum* of 1814 (Pius VII, 1814); the restored Society’s poet, Gerard Manley Hopkins, dead in 1889 and first published in 1918; and the twentieth century’s Ignatian minds—Erich Przywara, whose *Deus semper maior* remains in copyright in the United States into the 2030s (Przywara, 1938), Karl Rahner (Endean, 2001), Pierre Teilhard de Chardin. The boundary is historical, not accidental, and it is also a rights boundary: almost everything before 1773 is public domain in its original language, and almost everything of consequence after it is not. An apparatus owns its absences. These lie on the far side of a threshold this one has chosen not to cross.

The threshold of 1773 has its counterpart at the other end of the corpus, and the apparatus carries both boundary documents. The bull — Paul III’s approval of the ten companions on 27 September 1540, with their own sketch of a way of life, the Formula of the Institute, quoted whole inside the papal frame, and the famous restriction to sixty members, lifted four years later — is carried complete, in the Latin of the 1892 *Institutum Societatis Iesu* with an unofficial working translation, its paragraphs numbered on this site’s own grid at the print’s marginal breaks. With it the corpus opens and closes on papal parchment: what *Regimini militantis Ecclesiae* set in motion in 1540, *Dominus ac Redemptor* ended in 1773, and everything else the corpus carries lies between the two.

A second boundary runs through the shelf itself, and it should be stated as plainly as the first. Four modern translations—George Ganss’s *Exercises* of 1992 and his *Constitutions* as revised under John Padberg in 1996, Parmananda Divarkar’s *Pilgrim’s Testament* of 1995, and Joseph Munitiz’s *Spiritual Diary* of 1987—are in copyright, and they are the editions scholarship cites. Their structure, their statistics and their canonical anchors are part of every function of the site; their running text is not shipped and never will be. A reader who owns one of them opens it from a PDF in the browser; the file is read by pdf.js, stored in that browser alone, and never uploaded; only the passages that local retrieval selects for a specific question are sent onward. This is the apparatus’s second rights-fact: what the public domain provides is carried whole—the trilingual *Exercises*, the letters of 1524–1547, the *Directory* of 1599, Favre’s *Memoriale*, Xavier, Pascal, the *Monita*, the brief—and what it does not provide is bounded, not paraphrased.

abschnitte.titel: The Apparatus: Editions, Citation, and Limits
paras: *Ignatiana* is a static website with no build step, no accounts and no tracking, and a single optional server function—the citation-bound dialogue described below; its data files, build scripts and editorial method are open in the accompanying repository, archived with a digital object identifier (Fassbender, 2026a). Each shipped module is a reading edition prepared from a stated source: the *Monumenta Ignatiana* of 1919 for the Spanish, Latin and Directory texts (Ignatius of Loyola, 1919); Mullan (1914) and Longridge (1919) for the English of the *Exercises*; O’Leary’s volume of 1914 for the letters; Bouix’s editio princeps of 1873 for Favre; Coleridge (1872), M’Crie (Pascal, 1656–1657/1856), Brownlee (1857) and Theiner (Clement XIV, 1773/1852) for the outer lines—in every case reconstructed from the optical character recognition of a public scan and emended against the page images, with the residue of scanning error left visible rather than silently corrected. Works written in Spanish or Latin are presented bilingually. Where a public-domain English translation exists it is used and named; where none exists—for the *Directory* as an alternative to Longridge, for Favre, for the *Imago* epigrams and for the brief of 1773—the site supplies working translations of its own, marked as such, carrying no ecclesiastical or scholarly authority, and dedicated to the public domain. The rule for scholarly use is printed on every relevant page: cite the original.

The organizing discipline of the apparatus is the citation grid. Every paragraph carries a stable identifier in the form native to its work: the *Exercises* by the bracketed numbers [1]–[370] that Arturo Codina introduced in his edition of 1928 and that every modern edition has kept; the *Constitutions* by their bracketed paragraphs [1]–[827]; the memoir by [1]–[101]; the *Diary* by the continuous editorial numbering; the *Directory* by chapter and marginal paragraph; the letters by their number in the 1914 volume; Pascal by letter, the *Monita* by chapter and article, the brief by Theiner’s paragraphs. Where a numbering is the site’s own—Favre’s *Memoriale*, whose canonical *MF* numbers could not be reproduced from the 1873 print—the method page says so, and a citation of the site should name it as the source of the numbering. The Codina grid itself is editorial: it appears in none of the public-domain printings and was assigned here to the Autograph, the *Vulgata* and Mullan and validated for completeness, 370 of 370 in all three languages. On this grid rest the apparatus’s 2,464 canonical anchors: 1,768 tie paragraph numbers to the pages on which they begin in the locked reference editions, so that a concordance hit reads *SpEx* [23] or *Const* [134] rather than a page number nobody cites, while the shipped editions carry their numbers paragraph by paragraph and need no page index. The anchor table is released as a public-domain dataset because a citation index that others cannot build on is of little use.

On the grid rest the research instruments. A concordance searches every shipped text at once, and—once the reader has opened their own copies—the locked works too, with keyword in context, hit distribution per work and a canonical citation on every line. A discernment lexicon follows twenty-seven terms of the vocabulary of consolation, desolation and election across the corpus, with their distribution; it is here that the differences between the works become visible rather than merely assertable—tears belong almost entirely to the *Diary*, *discreet charity* almost entirely to the *Constitutions*. A concept atlas joins two terms when they occur in the same sentence more often than chance allows, coloured by the work in which each has its centre of gravity, so that the seams between manual, journal and law appear as regions of a graph; keyness per work is computed by the log-likelihood measure (Dunning, 1993), and both atlas and keyness are offered as finding aids, not as semantic claims. Registers of persons and places, the memoir’s itinerary, and a co-occurrence network of the correspondence complete the set. Six curated reading paths—the Four Weeks, the discernment of spirits, the election, Ignatius governing by letter, the Society’s image, and the Society as culture—give a stated order, a reason for every station, and a guiding question to carry into the text.

The last instrument is the one that most needs a warning. The citation-bound dialogue is a retrieval-augmented conversation (Lewis et al., 2020) in which a retrieval running in the reader’s browser selects the paragraphs bearing on a question, and a language model is required to answer from those passages alone, with a canonical citation attached to every substantive claim; it refuses to assert what the passages do not carry. It is still a language model and can misread. Every citation it gives can and should be checked against the edition, and the apparatus makes that check a matter of one click precisely so that it will be made. One disclosure belongs here because it concerns the whole and not a module: the apparatus was built in sustained working sessions with a large language model, under an editor who takes responsibility for every selection, emendation and working translation, and the commit history of the repository records, stage by stage, what was built, corrected and reconsidered. A corpus about the discernment of spirits, assembled partly by a machine whose motions must themselves be tested, owes its readers this fact plainly stated.

The limits are stated as plainly as the method. These are selections chosen for an argument about how a method of discernment was made, taught and contested, not complete works: the letters are twenty-four of nearly seven thousand; Pascal is three letters of eighteen; Xavier is four letters; Acosta is eleven chapters of a seven-book work, in a 1604 translation whose freedoms are its own; Ricci/Trigault is eight sections of Purchas’s 1625 digest, an abridgement whose cuts are Purchas’s and not this site’s; the *Relations* are four selections of seventy-three volumes; Muratori is five chapters of twenty-odd, in a 1759 London English made from the French, and Montoya four passages of a book-length relation; the *Musurgia* is thirteen paragraphs of a work of more than a thousand folio pages, chosen to show the architecture, the birds and the affects rather than the theory of composition that fills the middle books; the Pozzo module is fourteen paragraphs of a two-volume plate-book, its Fig. 90 abridged to its argument as its note discloses, and its English is the print's own translation of 1707, not this site's; the limpieza module carries three decrees and one memorial — the legislation and the dissent of a single decade — and names rather than carries Ribadeneira's covering letters and the abrogation of 1946, which falls outside the corpus's public-domain rule; the Ratio of 1599 is two rule-series of a document that regulates thirty offices, in a working translation; the Coimbra module is the Prooemium of a commentary that runs to several hundred columns; the Suárez module is three chapters of a commentary of six books, in a nineteenth-century reprint of the posthumous text — not the autograph lectures the modern critical edition prints — with its scan errors emended against sense; the *Imago* is twenty-three pages across its Latin and Dutch printings; the *Cautio* is two dubia of fifty-one, the *Trutznachtigall* two poems of some fifty, Nadal is one text of a large body, Rodríguez is one treatise of the twenty-four — in a translation made, moreover, from the French rather than the Spanish — and the Caussade is carried in Ramière’s arrangement of 1861, which modern criticism regards as an edited text of debated authorship, not an autograph. The 1914 letters are an optical scan whose errors are left visible. Name recognition is automatic, over-recognizes liturgical capitalization and under-recognizes Spanish and Basque names. The *Complementary Norms* are not separated out as an independent citation series. The readability and complexity measures were removed from the apparatus by design; only the keyness comparison remains, and it describes the seven core works only. The itinerary follows the memoir’s own account, which is a narrative composed thirty years after the events and shaped for a purpose (McManamon, 2013). The working translations are honest and consistent in their key terms, and they are the work of a machine. Corrections are welcome through the repository, and errors in the anchor table especially so: a wrong anchor produces a wrong citation, which is the one failure mode this instrument must not have.

The recurring discovery of this corpus is that the Ignatian tradition is unusually well documented at exactly the point where most spiritual traditions are silent: the point where a private experience becomes a teachable method. The convalescent at Loyola noticed that two kinds of thought left two kinds of aftertaste (Autobiog. [8]); the manual turned the observation into fourteen rules (SpEx [313]–[327]); the *Diary* shows the rules being applied by their author to a decision about money, over forty days, with the tears counted (Diary [1]–[34]); the *Directory* codified how a stranger should be led through the same rules without being pushed (Dir. 1599, c. XXIV [1]); Favre’s journal shows the rules at work on an ordinary Tuesday; the letters show them administered as “community medicine” to a house of over-fervent students (Letters, no. 24); Spee shows them turned against a legal procedure; and Pascal shows what their critics feared they would become. The apparatus exists so that these eight statements can be checked, sentence by sentence, against the texts—and so that a ninth, which a reader may wish to make, can be checked too.

The site’s name is a plural: *Ignatiana*, the things of Ignatius, in the old bibliographical sense of a collection of documents gathered around a person. It is also a method. The *Exercises* end with a set of rules for “thinking with the Church” and begin with a *Presupposition* (SpEx [22]) that every good Christian should be more ready to save a neighbour’s proposition than to condemn it, and, if it cannot be saved, should ask how the neighbour understands it. A corpus with exact citation is the philological form of that presupposition. The texts are here—whole where the public domain allows, anchored where it does not, numbered throughout, searchable at once. When disputes arise about what the tradition actually said, ask how the text understands it, and cite the paragraph.
